newsitem.title: JAPAN: Olympics-Higher downhill start fine for TV, CBS says.
newsitem.headline: Olympics-Higher downhill start fine for TV, CBS says.

text.p: U.S. network CBS said on Sunday it would have no trouble covering the 1998 Winter Olympic men's downhill in Nagano, whatever the eventual height of the starting line.
"Television is portable," said Joe Peterson, CBS Olympic venues production manager. "We don't need buildings to do television."
The American network has paid a record $375 million for the U.S. broadcasting rights to the 1998 Winter Olympics to be held in Nagano, Japan.
A dispute started when local organisers refused a request by the International Ski Federation (FIS) to raise the start of the course in Hakuba, 50 km west of Nagano, to 1,800 metres above sea level.
They said a higher start would encroach on a national park, where Japanese law prohibits construction of permanent buildings.

Last week, Nagano Organising Committee director general Makato Kobayashi told Reuters that an Olympic downhill start required permanent structures to provide firm positions for television cameras, start gates, pipes and timing devices.
Kobayashi said the start would remain at 1,680 metres. "Were just not going to move the starting point. That's it. End of story."

After test events held last year, the FIS found the proposed course was too short and said it would prefer a higher start. It said it would start the race on snow without a start hut or other permanent structures if need be.
Kobayashi dismissed the idea. "What if the snow melts a little or shifts a bit?" he said.
Competitors would not tolerate starts from temporary structures such as tents, he said. "The athletes would be up in arms."
Kobayashi also said that connecting the two sections of the course would be difficult as they are separated by a pond. Recreational skiers use both areas but they are unconnected, he said.
Peterson said CBS normally used two cameras to cover downhill starts: one hand-held camera just beyond the start gates and a point-of-view camera mounted on the start hut.
But if there were no start hut, CBS could improvise, said Peterson, who is in Nagano preparing for the network's Olympic coverage.
